the contribution of the different energy systems during 200-1500-m running depends on the distance, the speed, and the training status of the athletes.
the energy systems are recruited differently during 200- and 1500-m runs.

1) the contribution of energy sources during 1500-m to 200-m running in highly-trained athletes is similar to that in untrained athletes, but the relative contribution of anaerobic energy sources is higher, and 2) the contribution of anaerobically produced ATP to total energy production increases as a function of running velocity and decreases as a function of the duration of the running event.

the contribution of the different energy systems to running performance.
the energy system contribution during 100- to 150-m sprint running in highly trained runners.
the energy contribution to running in highly trained male athletes during 200- and 1500-m races.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the contribution of the anaerobic system is not constant throughout the 200-m to 1500 m range.
the energy contribution of the aerobic and anaerobic energy systems during 200-1500-m running is highly dependent on the intensity of exercise and the duration of exercise.

the anaerobic energy system is the primary energy system utilized in the 200m, the anaerobic and aerobic energy systems are both equally utilized in the 400m and 800m and the aerobic energy system is the only energy system utilized in 1500m.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
energy system contribution is not constant throughout 200 to 1500 m running.
there are two distinct energy systems at work during running.

there are no differences between 1500-m and 200-m running for the contribution of the energy system, and that the contribution of the anaerobic lactic energy system increases with increasing running distance.

the energy contribution from the anaerobic energy systems is much greater than previously reported, and this is true even at the 1500-m distance.
the contribution of different energy systems during 200 to 1500 m running varies with race distance, with a greater contribution of the anaerobic energy system as race distance decreases.
the energy system contributions during 200-1500 m running in highly trained endurance runners are not as different as previously thought.
